screens.title: Serverless Application Development and Deployment with SAM and CDK
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will see why Infrastructure as Code is essential for real serverless applications and how the AWS Serverless Application Model and the AWS Cloud Development Kit let you define the same architecture in two different ways. We'll compare declarative templates that extend CloudFormation with SAM to programmatic stacks you write in a language like Python with CDK. You'll follow a concrete example: a Lambda-based A P I that reads and writes items to a DynamoDB table. We'll show a SAM template that wires the function, table, and A P I together, and a short Python Lambda that implements POST and GET behavior. You will also see the SAM CLI workflow for local testing, building and guided deployment, and a brief CDK snippet that generates equivalent CloudFormation. Finally, we'll outline common mistakes you should watch for, like IAM permissions and environment variable wiring. By the end you'll understand the trade-offs and have a practical path for developing, testing, and deploying serverless systems with repeatable IaC.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the practical outcomes of this chapter. First, you will understand why Infrastructure as Code is essential for serverless applications: it makes multi-resource systems reproducible, testable, and manageable in version control. Second, you will learn how to define serverless resources using AWS SAM templates, including the Transform declaration, Resources, Events, and Policies sections. Third, you'll be able to deploy and manage serverless applications with the SAM CLI, using build and guided deploy flows that package code and create CloudFormation stacks. Fourth, you will explore AWS CDK as an alternative that lets you write code to construct the same resources, which is valuable when you need loops, abstractions, or programmatic reuse. Each objective pairs a specific skill with why it matters in production and a short mnemonic to help you remember the workflow.

screens.title: Infrastructure as Code for Serverless
screens.narratorSegment: Infrastructure as Code means managing cloud resources through files that live in version control instead of making ad hoc changes in the console. For serverless applications this is especially important because real systems usually span many resources: multiple Lambda functions, A P I Gateway routes, DynamoDB tables, SQS queues, and permissions that connect them. When you write those resources as code you gain three practical advantages. First, repeatability: builds and deployments produce the same stack across environments, so staging mirrors production. Second, reviewability: code can be peer-reviewed in a pull request, revealing missing IAM permissions or misconfigured event mappings before deployment. Third, automation: CI/CD pipelines can synthesize and deploy stacks automatically. A common misconception is that IaC is only for large teams — in fact, even small projects benefit immediately from tracking resource changes and rollbacks. Example: instead of manually creating a table and a function in the console, you declare a DynamoDB table and a Lambda function with an A P I event in a single template. That single source of truth reduces misconfiguration and supports rollback if a deploy fails. Think of IaC as the single authoritative description of your serverless system — ask yourself how you would recover or reproduce the system tomorrow if a resource were accidentally deleted.

content.html:
Core Concept › Infrastructure as Code
What IaC means for serverless
Declare functions, tables, queues, and permissions in a template or programmatic stack so deployments are predictable and auditable.
Key benefit
Repeatable environments for staging and production.
Common-mistake
Treating console changes as authoritative and not capturing them in code.
Key Takeaway

IaC is the single source of truth for serverless systems; it makes collaboration and CI/CD possible.

Analogy and Example
Think of IaC like a recipe: a single document tells anyone how to recreate the dish. For serverless, the recipe lists the tables, functions, and event bindings so rollout is consistent.
Console approach
Click to create a function, then a table, then set permissions. Hard to reproduce.
IaC approach
A template or stack declares all resources; run build and deploy to reproduce the environment.
Check your understanding
  • Why does version control matter for serverless resources?
  • What risk do manual console changes introduce?
  • How does IaC support rollback?

screens.title: SAM Templates: template.yaml Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: The AWS Serverless Application Model is a concise extension of CloudFormation designed specifically for serverless resources. The key entry point is template. yaml. It declares a Transform to let CloudFormation know you're using SAM's shorthand. Under Resources you declare a DynamoDB table as a SimpleTable, a Lambda function as AWS::Serverless::Function, and Events that map A P I Gateway paths to function invocations. Policies in SAM allow you to request common managed policies such as DynamoDBReadWritePolicy that grant the Lambda role explicit permissions to the table. A concrete example is a template that defines a table with a string primary key, a function that points to a CodeUri directory, environment variables that pass the table name to the function, and an Api event mapping Path /items to the function. When you read such a template, look for four things: resource identifiers, property wiring (for example environment variables and handler), event definitions that establish triggers, and policies that define permissions. A common pitfall is an incorrect CodeUri path; that causes build and deploy to fail because SAM cannot find your function code. The template is your contract: keep it minimal, explicit, and in version control.

keyIdea.title: SAM template essentials
keyIdea.text: Transform signals SAM usage; Resources declare services; Events map triggers; Policies grant the Lambda permissions it needs.

content.html:
Definition › SAM template.yaml
template.yaml (annotated)
This sample shows the Transform, Resources and Outputs you will commonly use for a Lambda + API + DynamoDB workflow.
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Description: A simple serverless API with Lambda and DynamoDB

Parameters:
  TableName:
    Type: String
    Default: MyServerlessTable

Resources:
  MyDynamoDBTable:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::SimpleTable
    Properties:
      TableName: !Ref TableName
      PrimaryKey:
        Name: id
        Type: String

  MyApiFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Handler: app.lambda_handler
      Runtime: python3.9
      CodeUri: ./my_api_function
      Environment:
        Variables:
          TABLE_NAME: !Ref MyDynamoDBTable
      Events:
        ApiEvent:
          Type: Api
          Properties:
            Path: /items
            Method: any

Outputs:
  ApiEndpoint:
    Value: !Sub "https://${ServerlessRestApi}.execute-api.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com/Prod/items"
Explainer cards
Transform
Signals that SAM's serverless shorthand will be expanded into CloudFormation resources at deploy time.
Resources
Declare the table and function. Note environment variables and CodeUri are critical wiring points.
Events & Policies
Events map API routes to functions. Policies grant managed permissions like DynamoDB read-write to the function role.
Common mistake

A wrong CodeUri path or missing policy will cause build or permission failures during deployment.

screens.title: Lambda Function: app.py Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the example Lambda function that implements a simple A P I for items. The function reads the table name from an environment variable, constructs a DynamoDB table resource using the SDK, and inspects the incoming HTTP method and path. For a POST to the items path it parses the request body, creates an item with an id and data field, and calls put_item to write to the table, returning a created response. For a GET it uses a table scan and returns the set of items. Two practical points matter here: first, environment variables are the recommended way to pass resource identifiers like the table name into your Lambda, so you do not hard-code environment-specific values. Second, scan is convenient for examples but is not efficient at scale; in production you would use queries and proper indexing. A common misconception is that local testing behavior always matches cloud behavior. For example, local DynamoDB emulators or IAM contexts may differ, so verify the deployed stack. This code is intentionally simple so you can focus on how the Lambda integrates with the rest of the stack, and to show where permissions and configuration must match what is declared in the template.

keyIdea.title: Function behavior
keyIdea.text: Use environment variables for configuration; ensure IAM permissions match the function's DynamoDB operations.

content.html:
Definition › Lambda app.py
Lambda code (example)
import json
import os
import boto3

dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb')
table_name = os.environ['TABLE_NAME']
table = dynamodb.Table(table_name)

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    http_method = event['httpMethod']
    path = event['path']

    if http_method == 'POST' and path == '/items':
        body = json.loads(event['body'])
        item = {'id': body['id'], 'data': body.get('data', 'default')}
        table.put_item(Item=item)
        return {
            'statusCode': 201,
            'body': json.dumps({'message': 'Item created', 'item': item})
        }
    elif http_method == 'GET' and path == '/items':
        response = table.scan()
        return {
            'statusCode': 200,
            'body': json.dumps(response['Items'])
        }
    else:
        return {
            'statusCode': 400,
            'body': json.dumps({'message': 'Invalid request'})
        }
Explanation cards
Environment variables
TABLE_NAME is passed from the template so the same code runs across environments without changes.
Permissions
The function must have DynamoDB read and write permissions; grant them via SAM policies or CDK table grants.
Production note
Use queries and keys for production read patterns instead of scanning large tables.
Pro tip

Log structured events during local testing to compare emulator behavior with cloud logs.

screens.title: SAM CLI Workflow: build and deploy
screens.narratorSegment: The SAM CLI supports a reproducible workflow you can follow on every serverless project. Start by initializing a project or creating your template and function code. The build step packages your function and dependencies into an artifact the deployment system can use. Running sam build creates a packaged folder structure that CloudFormation can consume. Next, sam deploy --guided walks you through stack name, region, and S3 bucket choices and saves those settings to a configuration file so future deploys are non-interactive. Under the hood, SAM transforms the template into standard CloudFormation and uploads artifacts to S3 before creating or updating a stack. A practical example: after you replace generated skeleton files with your template. yaml and app dot P Y file, run sam build to prepare the code, then sam deploy --guided to create a CloudFormation stack named MyServerlessAppStack. A common misconception is that sam deploy directly modifies live resources without rollback — SAM uses CloudFormation, so you get change sets, stack events, and the ability to inspect failures. Always watch the deploy output and CloudFormation events to understand resource creation steps and to recover from failures.

content.html:
Process Flow › SAM CLI workflow
Steps
1. Initialize or prepare project
Create template.yaml and the function code directory structure.
2. Build
Run sam build to package dependencies and create a .aws-sam artifact directory ready for deployment.
3. Deploy guided
Run sam deploy --guided to select stack name, region, and let SAM upload artifacts and create a CloudFormation stack.
Terminal examples
sam init --runtime python3.9 --name my-serverless-app sam build sam deploy --guided
Key Takeaway

SAM produces CloudFormation stacks; monitor stack events to understand resource creation and failures.

screens.title: Local Testing and Debugging with SAM CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Local testing accelerates development by letting you exercise Lambda functions and A P I routes without deploying to AWS. The SAM CLI exposes two useful commands. First, sam local invoke lets you run a single function with a synthetic event file; pass an event. json that mimics the A P I Gateway request and inspect the returned response. Second, sam local start-api starts a local HTTP endpoint that emulates A P I Gateway. You can use curl or a browser to POST and GET against that endpoint, getting immediate feedback and faster iteration. There is also sam local start-lambda for testing other event sources. If you want to attach a debugger, sam local invoke supports a debug port so you can connect from your IDE. Remember a critical contrast: local emulation does not replicate every IAM, network, or managed service behavior. For example, if your function relies on IAM roles created at deploy time or on specific AWS managed platform behavior, the local run may not expose those exact conditions. A practical example: create an event. json for a POST containing an id and data field, run sam local invoke to ensure your JSON parsing and DynamoDB client calls behave as expected, then start the local A P I and try a curl POST followed by a GET to confirm end-to-end behavior. Always follow local tests with a deployed integration test when possible.

Process Flow › Local Testing & Debugging
Key commands
sam local invoke
Invoke a function with an event file to validate logic and return values.
sam local start-api
Start a local HTTP server that emulates API Gateway so curl or a browser can hit your endpoints.
Example event.json and curl
{ "httpMethod": "POST", "path": "/items", "body": "{\"id\": \"item-local\", \"data\": \"local-value\"}" } # After starting local API # curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"id":"item-local","data":"local-value"}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/items # curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/items
Warning

Local emulation cannot perfectly replicate IAM contexts and managed service nuances; always run a deployed integration test before trusting production behavior.

screens.title: AWS CDK: Programmatic Infrastructure
screens.narratorSegment: The AWS Cloud Development Kit lets you describe infrastructure using a general purpose programming language. Instead of writing YAML, you write constructs that create resources programmatically. This is powerful when you need loops, conditional logic, or reusable constructs to create many similar resources. A compact CDK Python snippet defines a DynamoDB table, a Lambda function with environment variables, grants read-write permissions, creates an A P I Gateway that proxies requests, and outputs an A P I endpoint. The workflow differs: you run cdk synth to generate a CloudFormation template, inspect the synthesized template, and then run cdk deploy to create the stack. The CDK still produces CloudFormation under the hood, so troubleshooting uses the same CloudFormation events and stack outputs. Use CDK when you need to encapsulate patterns into reusable classes or when a code-first approach simplifies complex architectures. A common misconception is that CDK eliminates CloudFormation; in reality it generates CloudFormation, so you must still understand the resulting resources and permissions. CDK is a lower-friction way to build abstractions, but always inspect synthesized templates to confirm resource shapes before deploying to production.

keyIdea.title: CDK advantage
keyIdea.text: Use CDK to programmatically define resources when you need loops, constructs, or reusable stacks; it synthesizes to CloudFormation for deployment.

content.html:
Definition › AWS CDK (Python example)
CDK snippet
from aws_cdk import (
    Stack,
    aws_lambda as _lambda,
    aws_apigateway as apigw,
    aws_dynamodb as dynamodb,
    CfnOutput
)
from constructs import Construct

class MyServerlessAppStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope: Construct, construct_id: str, **kwargs) -> None:
        super().__init__(scope, construct_id, **kwargs)

        table = dynamodb.Table(
            self, "MyServerlessTable",
            partition_key=dynamodb.Attribute(name="id", type=dynamodb.AttributeType.STRING),
            read_capacity=1,
            write_capacity=1
        )

        api_function = _lambda.Function(
            self, "MyApiFunction",
            runtime=_lambda.Runtime.PYTHON_3_9,
            handler="app.lambda_handler",
            code=_lambda.Code.from_asset("my_api_function"),
            environment={"TABLE_NAME": table.table_name}
        )

        table.grant_read_write_data(api_function)

        api = apigw.LambdaRestApi(self, "MyApi", handler=api_function, proxy=True)

        CfnOutput(self, "ApiEndpoint", value=api.url_for_path("/items"))
When to choose CDK
Choose CDK when you need programmatic patterns, custom constructs, or when many resources share similar configuration. It reduces duplication through code abstractions.

screens.title: Integrating Lambda with API Gateway, DynamoDB, and SQS
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless applications are integrations: Lambda functions respond to events from A P I Gateway, SQS, or stream sources, and they read or write state to DynamoDB. IaC makes these integrations explicit. For example, a SAM function resource can define an Api event that maps the /items path to the function, while a policy block grants DynamoDB read-write access for the table. In CDK the same pattern appears as a LambdaRestApi construct wired to a function and a table. grant_read_write_data call that changes the function's role. For queue-based processing, you declare an SQS queue in the template and add an SQS event source to the Lambda, or in CDK you add an SQS event source subscription. The essential teaching point is that triggers and permissions must be declared together so the deployment creates the correct IAM role with least privilege. A common mistake is granting overly broad permissions or forgetting to grant any permissions, which results in runtime authorization errors. A practical scenario: when you want to accept HTTP input and persist it, declare the A P I path, the Lambda function, the DynamoDB table, and a managed policy for read-write access all in the same template or stack. This avoids a disconnect where the code assumes a table exists but the deployed role lacks access.

Integration cards
API Gateway
Use Api events in SAM or LambdaRestApi in CDK to expose HTTP endpoints that trigger Lambda functions.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Several mistakes recur when teams move to IaC for serverless. First, IAM permissions: forgetting to grant your function access to DynamoDB or SQS is the most common runtime failure. The fix is to declare explicit managed policies in SAM or grant methods in CDK so the function role includes only needed actions. Second, environment variables: failing to pass resource names to your function leads to hard-coded values or runtime failures; ensure the table name or bucket name is provided in the template. Third, CodeUri path errors during sam build or deploy are simple but time-consuming: validate your local paths and packaging before deploying. Fourth, local testing discrepancies: sam local emulates A P I Gateway and Lambda but does not replicate every aspect of the managed cloud environment; always run an integration test in a deployed stack. A frequent misconception is that local success guarantees production success. To avoid these pitfalls adopt a checklist: confirm policies, confirm environment variables are set, verify CodeUri resolves, and run a deploy-validation step. When you see an error during deploy, inspect CloudFormation events — they tell you which resource failed and why. These practices shorten troubleshooting and reduce deployment surprises.

screens.title: Hands-on: Deploy MyServerlessApp with SAM CLI
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough follows the chapter's activity and shows the commands and checks you will run. Start by creating a project directory and a function folder. Add the provided template. yaml and app dot P Y file into the appropriate locations. Next run sam build; this packages your code into a. aws-sam folder. Then run sam deploy --guided: the CLI will ask for a stack name, region, and whether you want it to create IAM roles. Choose a stack name like MyServerlessAppStack and allow role creation if you do not manage roles separately. After deployment completes the SAM CLI prints the ApiEndpoint output. Verify deployments with curl: send a POST with a JSON body containing an id and data to the items path, then request GET to list items. For local testing, create an event. json that represents the POST payload and run sam local invoke to test the handler, or run sam local start-api and use curl against the local endpoint. Finally, clean up by deleting the CloudFormation stack using the AWS CLI or the CloudFormation console. A useful habit is to save arguments to samconfig. toml so future deployments are automatic and repeatable. This sequence builds confidence and reinforces the repeatability that IaC provides.

screens.title: SAM vs CDK: When to Use Each
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between SAM and CDK depends on your project needs. SAM is a concise serverless-first extension of CloudFormation that makes templates shorter and maps common serverless patterns to simple YAML fragments. It shines when your team prefers declarative templates and you want direct control over CloudFormation outputs. CDK is best when you want to use programming constructs: loops to generate many similar resources, abstractions to encapsulate patterns, or language features for conditional configuration. Both approaches synthesize to CloudFormation and both support the same AWS resources and deployment model. A common misconception is that CDK removes CloudFormation; it does not — it generates CloudFormation templates that you can inspect. If you need reuse and programmatic generation, pick CDK. If you prefer compact, readable serverless-focused templates and want to use SAM CLI's local testing features, pick SAM. In many projects teams use both: SAM for quick serverless templates and CDK to wrap larger application-level patterns. The pragmatic approach is to align tooling with team skills and maintainability goals, and to make sure your CI/CD pipeline enforces templates or stacks as the source of truth for deployments.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will see why Infrastructure as Code is essential for real serverless applications and how the AWS Serverless Application Model and the AWS Cloud Development Kit let you define the same architecture in two different ways. We'll compare declarative templates that extend CloudFormation with SAM to programmatic stacks you write in a language like Python with CDK. You'll follow a concrete example: a Lambda-based A P I that reads and writes items to a DynamoDB table. We'll show a SAM template that wires the function, table, and A P I together, and a short Python Lambda that implements POST and GET behavior. You will also see the SAM CLI workflow for local testing, building and guided deployment, and a brief CDK snippet that generates equivalent CloudFormation. Finally, we'll outline common mistakes you should watch for, like IAM permissions and environment variable wiring. By the end you'll understand the trade-offs and have a practical path for developing, testing, and deploying serverless systems with repeatable IaC.

These objectives guide the practical outcomes of this chapter. First, you will understand why Infrastructure as Code is essential for serverless applications: it makes multi-resource systems reproducible, testable, and manageable in version control. Second, you will learn how to define serverless resources using AWS SAM templates, including the Transform declaration, Resources, Events, and Policies sections. Third, you'll be able to deploy and manage serverless applications with the SAM CLI, using build and guided deploy flows that package code and create CloudFormation stacks. Fourth, you will explore AWS CDK as an alternative that lets you write code to construct the same resources, which is valuable when you need loops, abstractions, or programmatic reuse. Each objective pairs a specific skill with why it matters in production and a short mnemonic to help you remember the workflow.

This second objectives screen focuses on practice and integration. You will be able to declare event sources and policies so Lambda functions securely interact with A P I Gateway, DynamoDB, and SQS. Practical skills include passing configuration via environment variables so functions know the table name or bucket name at runtime. You will practice the SAM CLI local commands that emulate A P I Gateway and Lambda runtime behavior and know when local emulation diverges from the cloud. The hands-on objective walks you through building, deploying, verifying with curl, and cleaning up resources. Finally, you'll demonstrate understanding by answering assessment-style questions that ask you to choose between SAM, CDK, and CloudFormation based on use case. These objectives are deliberately practical: the aim is not only to read templates but to run, test, and iterate until deployments are repeatable and debuggable.

Infrastructure as Code means managing cloud resources through files that live in version control instead of making ad hoc changes in the console. For serverless applications this is especially important because real systems usually span many resources: multiple Lambda functions, A P I Gateway routes, DynamoDB tables, SQS queues, and permissions that connect them. When you write those resources as code you gain three practical advantages. First, repeatability: builds and deployments produce the same stack across environments, so staging mirrors production. Second, reviewability: code can be peer-reviewed in a pull request, revealing missing IAM permissions or misconfigured event mappings before deployment. Third, automation: CI/CD pipelines can synthesize and deploy stacks automatically. A common misconception is that IaC is only for large teams — in fact, even small projects benefit immediately from tracking resource changes and rollbacks. Example: instead of manually creating a table and a function in the console, you declare a DynamoDB table and a Lambda function with an A P I event in a single template. That single source of truth reduces misconfiguration and supports rollback if a deploy fails. Think of IaC as the single authoritative description of your serverless system — ask yourself how you would recover or reproduce the system tomorrow if a resource were accidentally deleted.

The AWS Serverless Application Model is a concise extension of CloudFormation designed specifically for serverless resources. The key entry point is template. yaml. It declares a Transform to let CloudFormation know you're using SAM's shorthand. Under Resources you declare a DynamoDB table as a SimpleTable, a Lambda function as AWS::Serverless::Function, and Events that map A P I Gateway paths to function invocations. Policies in SAM allow you to request common managed policies such as DynamoDBReadWritePolicy that grant the Lambda role explicit permissions to the table. A concrete example is a template that defines a table with a string primary key, a function that points to a CodeUri directory, environment variables that pass the table name to the function, and an Api event mapping Path /items to the function. When you read such a template, look for four things: resource identifiers, property wiring (for example environment variables and handler), event definitions that establish triggers, and policies that define permissions. A common pitfall is an incorrect CodeUri path; that causes build and deploy to fail because SAM cannot find your function code. The template is your contract: keep it minimal, explicit, and in version control.

Let's walk through the example Lambda function that implements a simple A P I for items. The function reads the table name from an environment variable, constructs a DynamoDB table resource using the SDK, and inspects the incoming HTTP method and path. For a POST to the items path it parses the request body, creates an item with an id and data field, and calls put_item to write to the table, returning a created response. For a GET it uses a table scan and returns the set of items. Two practical points matter here: first, environment variables are the recommended way to pass resource identifiers like the table name into your Lambda, so you do not hard-code environment-specific values. Second, scan is convenient for examples but is not efficient at scale; in production you would use queries and proper indexing. A common misconception is that local testing behavior always matches cloud behavior. For example, local DynamoDB emulators or IAM contexts may differ, so verify the deployed stack. This code is intentionally simple so you can focus on how the Lambda integrates with the rest of the stack, and to show where permissions and configuration must match what is declared in the template.

The SAM CLI supports a reproducible workflow you can follow on every serverless project. Start by initializing a project or creating your template and function code. The build step packages your function and dependencies into an artifact the deployment system can use. Running sam build creates a packaged folder structure that CloudFormation can consume. Next, sam deploy --guided walks you through stack name, region, and S3 bucket choices and saves those settings to a configuration file so future deploys are non-interactive. Under the hood, SAM transforms the template into standard CloudFormation and uploads artifacts to S3 before creating or updating a stack. A practical example: after you replace generated skeleton files with your template. yaml and app dot P Y file, run sam build to prepare the code, then sam deploy --guided to create a CloudFormation stack named MyServerlessAppStack. A common misconception is that sam deploy directly modifies live resources without rollback — SAM uses CloudFormation, so you get change sets, stack events, and the ability to inspect failures. Always watch the deploy output and CloudFormation events to understand resource creation steps and to recover from failures.

Local testing accelerates development by letting you exercise Lambda functions and A P I routes without deploying to AWS. The SAM CLI exposes two useful commands. First, sam local invoke lets you run a single function with a synthetic event file; pass an event. json that mimics the A P I Gateway request and inspect the returned response. Second, sam local start-api starts a local HTTP endpoint that emulates A P I Gateway. You can use curl or a browser to POST and GET against that endpoint, getting immediate feedback and faster iteration. There is also sam local start-lambda for testing other event sources. Remember a critical contrast: local emulation does not replicate every IAM, network, or managed service behavior. For example, if your function relies on IAM roles created at deploy time or on specific AWS managed platform behavior, the local run may not expose those exact conditions. A practical example: create an event. json for a POST containing an id and data field, run sam local invoke to ensure your JSON parsing and DynamoDB client calls behave as expected, then start the local A P I and try a curl POST followed by a GET to confirm end-to-end behavior. Always follow local tests with a deployed integration test when possible.

The AWS Cloud Development Kit lets you describe infrastructure using a general purpose programming language. Instead of writing YAML, you write constructs that create resources programmatically. This is powerful when you need loops, conditional logic, or reusable constructs to create many similar resources. A compact CDK Python snippet defines a DynamoDB table, a Lambda function with environment variables, grants read-write permissions, creates an A P I Gateway that proxies requests, and outputs an A P I endpoint. The workflow differs: you run cdk synth to generate a CloudFormation template, inspect the synthesized template, and then run cdk deploy to create the stack. The CDK still produces CloudFormation under the hood, so troubleshooting uses the same CloudFormation events and stack outputs. Use CDK when you need to encapsulate patterns into reusable classes or when a code-first approach simplifies complex architectures. A common misconception is that CDK eliminates CloudFormation; in reality it generates CloudFormation, so you must still understand the resulting resources and permissions. CDK is a lower-friction way to build abstractions, but always inspect synthesized templates to confirm resource shapes before deploying to production.
